title: The Growth of Renewable Energy
passage: Renewable energy has become an increasingly important source of electricity in many countries. Unlike fossil fuels, renewable sources such as solar and wind power can produce energy with much lower greenhouse gas emissions. They can also reduce dependence on imported fuels and contribute to long-term energy security. However, the expansion of renewable energy requires investment in infrastructure, improvements in electricity storage, and policies that support the transition to cleaner energy systems.
reference: Renewable energy is becoming increasingly important because it produces electricity with lower emissions, reduces dependence on imported fuels, and improves energy security, although its expansion requires infrastructure investment, better storage, and supportive policies.
mainIdea: Renewable energy is increasingly important for cleaner electricity and energy security, but its expansion requires significant infrastructure and policy support.
keyPoints: Renewable energy produces electricity with lower greenhouse gas emissions.
It can reduce dependence on imported fuels and improve energy security.
Expanding renewable energy requires infrastructure, energy storage, and supportive policies.

title: The Importance of Urban Green Spaces
passage: Urban green spaces such as parks, gardens, and tree-lined streets provide important environmental and social benefits. Trees can reduce urban temperatures, absorb pollutants, and improve air quality, while parks provide residents with opportunities for exercise and relaxation. Green spaces may also encourage social interaction and strengthen communities. Nevertheless, maintaining these areas requires financial resources, careful planning, and long-term management, particularly in rapidly growing cities where land is limited.
reference: Urban green spaces improve environmental conditions, health, and community interaction by reducing heat and pollution and providing recreational areas, but their maintenance requires careful planning, funding, and long-term management.
mainIdea: Urban green spaces provide environmental, health, and social benefits, but maintaining them requires careful planning and resources.
keyPoints: Trees and green spaces can reduce heat and pollution and improve air quality.
Parks provide opportunities for exercise, relaxation, and social interaction.
Maintaining urban green spaces requires funding, planning, and long-term management.

title: The Role of Sleep in Learning
passage: Sleep plays a significant role in learning and memory. During sleep, the brain processes and organizes information acquired during the day, which can help strengthen newly formed memories. Research also suggests that insufficient sleep can reduce attention, concentration, and problem-solving ability. For students, therefore, regularly sacrificing sleep to study for longer periods may be counterproductive. A balanced routine that combines adequate sleep with effective study strategies can support both academic performance and overall well-being.
reference: Adequate sleep supports learning by strengthening memory and improving attention and problem-solving, whereas insufficient sleep can undermine academic performance, making a balanced study and sleep routine important for students.
mainIdea: Adequate sleep supports learning and academic performance, while insufficient sleep can negatively affect cognitive abilities.
keyPoints: Sleep helps the brain process information and strengthen memories.
Lack of sleep can reduce attention, concentration, and problem-solving ability.
Students benefit from balancing sufficient sleep with effective study strategies.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
passage: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in education to support both teachers and students. AI systems can provide personalized learning materials, identify areas where students are struggling, and offer immediate feedback on certain tasks. Teachers may also use these technologies to reduce administrative workloads and analyze student performance. However, the use of AI raises concerns about privacy, academic integrity, and excessive dependence on technology. Educational institutions therefore need clear policies that encourage responsible use while preserving the important role of teachers.
reference: Artificial intelligence can personalize learning, provide feedback, and reduce teachers' administrative workloads, but concerns about privacy, academic integrity, and technological dependence require institutions to establish clear policies for responsible use.
mainIdea: AI can provide important benefits in education, but its use requires responsible policies to address privacy and academic concerns.
keyPoints: AI can personalize learning and provide immediate feedback to students.
Teachers can use AI to reduce administrative work and analyze performance.
AI raises concerns about privacy, academic integrity, and dependence on technology.
Educational institutions need policies for responsible AI use.

title: The Benefits and Challenges of Remote Work
passage: Remote work has become more common as digital communication technologies have improved. Working from home can reduce commuting time, provide greater flexibility, and allow organizations to recruit employees from a wider geographical area. At the same time, remote workers may experience difficulties related to communication, isolation, and maintaining a clear separation between professional and personal life. Organizations can address some of these challenges by establishing clear communication practices, providing appropriate technology, and creating opportunities for employees to interact regularly.
reference: Remote work offers flexibility, saves commuting time, and expands recruitment opportunities, but communication, isolation, and work-life boundaries remain challenges that require effective organizational practices and technological support.
mainIdea: Remote work provides flexibility and other benefits but creates communication and work-life challenges that organizations must manage.
keyPoints: Remote work can reduce commuting time and provide greater flexibility.
Organizations can recruit employees from a wider geographical area.
Remote workers may experience communication problems, isolation, and work-life boundary difficulties.
Clear communication practices, technology, and regular interaction can address these challenges.

title: Water Conservation
passage: Growing populations and changing climate conditions are increasing pressure on freshwater resources in many regions. Agriculture is one of the largest users of freshwater, while households and industries also contribute significantly to water consumption. Improving irrigation systems, repairing leaks, recycling wastewater, and encouraging responsible consumption can reduce unnecessary water use. Effective conservation, however, requires cooperation among governments, businesses, farmers, and individuals because water management decisions in one sector can affect the availability of resources in others.
reference: Increasing pressure on freshwater resources requires conservation through efficient irrigation, leak prevention, wastewater recycling, and responsible consumption, supported by cooperation among governments, businesses, farmers, and individuals.
mainIdea: Increasing pressure on freshwater resources makes effective water conservation and cooperation among different sectors essential.
keyPoints: Population growth and climate conditions are increasing pressure on freshwater resources.
Agriculture, households, and industries are major users of freshwater.
Efficient irrigation, leak repair, wastewater recycling, and responsible consumption can reduce water use.
Effective conservation requires cooperation among governments, businesses, farmers, and individuals.

title: Public Transportation
passage: Efficient public transportation can provide significant economic and environmental benefits for cities. Buses, trains, and other forms of mass transit can reduce the number of private vehicles on roads, helping to decrease traffic congestion and air pollution. Reliable public transportation can also improve access to employment and education, particularly for people who cannot afford private vehicles. However, successful transportation systems require substantial investment, effective planning, and regular maintenance to ensure that services remain affordable, safe, and reliable.
reference: Efficient public transportation can reduce congestion and pollution while improving access to employment and education, but achieving these benefits requires substantial investment, effective planning, and reliable maintenance.
mainIdea: Efficient public transportation provides environmental and social benefits but requires substantial investment, planning, and maintenance.
keyPoints: Mass transit can reduce traffic congestion and air pollution.
Reliable public transportation can improve access to employment and education.
Effective transportation systems require investment, planning, and regular maintenance.

title: The Importance of Critical Thinking
passage: Critical thinking is an important skill in both education and the workplace because it enables people to evaluate information rather than simply accept it. Individuals who think critically can identify assumptions, compare different sources, recognize weak arguments, and use evidence when reaching conclusions. This skill has become particularly important as people encounter large amounts of information through digital media. Developing critical thinking requires practice, exposure to different perspectives, and the ability to distinguish reliable evidence from unsupported claims.
reference: Critical thinking enables people to evaluate information, identify assumptions, assess evidence, and recognize weak arguments, making it increasingly important in an environment where digital media provides large amounts of potentially unreliable information.
mainIdea: Critical thinking helps people evaluate information and evidence, making it increasingly important in the digital information environment.
keyPoints: Critical thinking allows people to evaluate information rather than simply accept it.
It involves identifying assumptions, comparing sources, recognizing weak arguments, and using evidence.
Digital media has increased the importance of critical thinking.
Developing this skill requires practice and exposure to different perspectives.

title: Technology and Healthcare
passage: Technological developments have transformed many aspects of healthcare. Electronic medical records can make patient information easier to access, while diagnostic technologies can help doctors identify diseases more accurately. Telemedicine has also expanded access to healthcare for people living far from medical facilities. Despite these advantages, healthcare organizations must address challenges involving data security, unequal access to technology, and the need to train medical professionals. Technology can therefore improve healthcare significantly, but its benefits depend on responsible implementation and appropriate support.
reference: Technology can improve healthcare through electronic records, accurate diagnosis, and telemedicine, but its benefits depend on addressing data security, unequal technological access, and professional training.
mainIdea: Technology can significantly improve healthcare and access to medical services, but its implementation must address security, access, and training challenges.
keyPoints: Electronic records improve access to patient information.
Diagnostic technologies can help doctors identify diseases more accurately.
Telemedicine can expand healthcare access for people far from medical facilities.
Healthcare organizations must address data security, unequal access, and professional training.

title: The Impact of Exercise
passage: Regular physical exercise contributes to both physical and mental health. Exercise can improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthen muscles and bones, and help people maintain a healthy body weight. It has also been associated with improved mood and reduced stress. Despite these benefits, many adults do not exercise regularly because of demanding work schedules, limited access to facilities, or a lack of motivation. Health experts therefore emphasize that even moderate activities, such as walking or cycling, can provide meaningful benefits when performed consistently.
reference: Regular exercise improves physical fitness, weight management, mood, and stress levels, but barriers such as busy schedules and limited access can prevent participation, making consistent moderate activity a practical approach.
mainIdea: Regular exercise provides important physical and mental health benefits, while consistent moderate activity can help overcome barriers to exercise.
keyPoints: Exercise improves cardiovascular fitness and strengthens muscles and bones.
It can help maintain healthy body weight and improve mood and stress levels.
Busy schedules, limited facilities, and lack of motivation can prevent regular exercise.
Consistent moderate activities such as walking or cycling can still provide meaningful benefits.

title: Food Waste in Developed Cities
passage: Around a third of the food produced in developed countries is never eaten. Much of this waste occurs in households, where shoppers buy more than they can consume, and in supermarkets, which routinely discard produce that is still perfectly edible. Several solutions have been proposed. Households can be given clearer information about storage and portion sizes, supermarkets can adjust their prices so that ripe produce is cheaper, and cities can make it easier for citizens to compost leftovers at home. Supporters of these measures argue that they would cut waste without asking households to change their diets.
mainIdea: A large share of food in developed countries is wasted, and reducing it mainly requires better storage information, cheaper pricing for ripe produce and easier home composting.
keyPoints: Roughly a third of the food produced in developed countries is never eaten.
Much of this waste happens in households and supermarkets, where produce is still edible when it is discarded.
Practical measures such as portion guidance, discounted ripe produce and home composting could reduce waste without changing diets.
reference: A third of the food produced in developed countries is thrown away, largely because households buy too much and supermarkets discard edible produce, so clearer storage guidance, cheaper prices for ripe items and easy home composting could cut this waste without any change in diet.

title: Remote Work and City Life
passage: Since the pandemic, many office workers have negotiated permanent hybrid arrangements, and city centres have felt the consequences. Buildings once busy every morning now stand empty for much of the day, while residential districts have seen demand for larger homes rise. Critics argue that this shift hollows out the commercial life of city centres and reduces the tax revenue that funds public transport. Supporters counter that fewer commuters mean cleaner air and that workers now value proximity to parks and schools far more than proximity to an office. Both sides agree that the balance will not return to what it was before 2020.
mainIdea: Hybrid working is permanently changing city life, harming busy city centres while improving air quality and changing what workers value.
keyPoints: Many office workers now have permanent hybrid arrangements and city-centre buildings are empty for much of the day.
Critics say this reduces the commercial life and tax revenue of city centres, which also funds public transport.
Supporters argue that fewer commuters mean cleaner air and that workers now prefer living near parks and schools.
reference: Hybrid working is permanently reshaping city life, leaving city-centre offices empty, cutting the tax revenue that funds public transport, and rewarding workers who now choose to live near parks and schools because the resulting reduction in commuters also means cleaner air.

title: Why Public Transport Needs Subsidies
passage: Buses and trains carry far more people per hour than private cars, yet in most cities the cheapest and most frequent option is still the one the driver pays for. Because fares usually cover only part of the real cost of running a service, operators rely on annual subsidies from city budgets. Cities that withdrew these subsidies rarely saved the money they expected, since the passengers who gave up their passes simply filled their cars and congested the roads instead. Transport economists therefore argue that public transport is not a service for those who ride it alone, but an infrastructure investment that benefits everyone who uses the street.
mainIdea: Fares never cover the real cost of public transport, so subsidies are justified because the benefits spread to the whole city through lower congestion, not only to passengers.
keyPoints: Fares normally cover only part of the real cost of running buses and trains, so operators depend on city subsidies.
Cities that cut subsidies rarely saved money because former passengers switched to cars and made congestion worse.
Economists therefore treat public transport as an infrastructure investment whose benefits reach everyone who uses the roads.
reference: Since fares cover only part of the real cost of running a service, public transport depends on subsidies, and withdrawing them rarely saves money because former passengers take to their cars, so economists treat the subsidy as an infrastructure investment whose lower congestion benefits the whole city.

title: The Rise of Online Health Advice
passage: An increasing number of people now look up their symptoms on their phones before consulting a doctor. Some doctors see this as harmless preparation, arguing that informed patients describe their symptoms more accurately. Others are more cautious, because self-diagnosis can encourage people to treat minor complaints with strong medication and to delay genuine emergencies. The evidence is mixed: studies suggest that online tools improve awareness of common conditions but perform poorly on unusual ones. Most experts now agree that the internet is a useful starting point rather than a replacement for professional care, particularly for children and older patients.
mainIdea: Online symptom checking is a useful first step that prepares patients and raises awareness, but it is unreliable for unusual conditions and must not replace professional care.
keyPoints: Many people now search their symptoms online before seeing a doctor, and some doctors see this as useful preparation.
Others warn that self-diagnosis can lead to strong medication for minor complaints and to delayed emergencies.
Evidence suggests these tools help with common conditions but perform poorly on unusual ones, so they are a starting point rather than a replacement.
reference: Searching symptoms online is a useful first step that helps patients describe their problem and raises awareness of common conditions, but because such tools perform poorly on unusual conditions and may lead to strong medication for minor complaints or delayed emergencies, they must never replace professional care.

title: School Start Times
passage: A growing number of secondary schools have moved their start time later, following research into adolescent sleep patterns. Pupils who begin at nine rather than eight are reported to be more attentive in morning lessons and perform better in examinations. Critics point out that such schedules complicate the lives of working parents, since older siblings may have to care for younger children before leaving home. Others argue that schools could solve this by adjusting the hours of clubs and transport instead. Despite the criticism, the evidence in favour of later starts continues to grow, and the trend is unlikely to reverse.
mainIdea: Later secondary school start times improve pupils’ attention and results because of adolescent sleep patterns, and the criticism about working parents has not stopped the trend.
keyPoints: Schools are moving later because research shows pupils who start at nine are more attentive and do better in examinations.
Critics argue that later starts complicate the lives of working parents who rely on older children for early childcare.
Defenders suggest clubs and transport could be rescheduled instead, and the trend is unlikely to reverse.
reference: Because research shows that pupils who start at nine are more attentive and perform better in examinations, later start times are spreading, and although critics point out that this complicates matters for working parents who depend on older children for early childcare, defenders propose rescheduling clubs and transport, so the trend is unlikely to reverse.

title: Banning Single-Use Plastics
passage: Several countries have banned the sale of plastic bags and disposable tableware, hoping to reduce the volume of waste that reaches the oceans. Environmental groups welcome these measures, pointing out that a single bag can persist for centuries and be eaten by marine animals. Retailers and packaging manufacturers have raised objections, arguing that alternatives are more expensive and that some replacements are made from materials that are just as damaging. Both sides agree that the waste problem is serious, but they disagree about whether a national ban is the most effective response to it.
mainIdea: Bans on single-use plastics reduce long-lasting ocean waste, but manufacturers and retailers dispute whether the alternatives are effective or affordable.
keyPoints: Several countries have banned plastic bags and disposable tableware to cut the waste reaching the oceans.
Environmental groups welcome this because a single bag can persist for centuries and be eaten by marine animals.
Manufacturers and retailers argue that alternatives cost more and are sometimes made from equally damaging materials.
reference: Although several countries have banned single-use plastics to reduce the long-lasting waste that reaches the oceans and harms marine animals, manufacturers and retailers dispute the measure, arguing that the alternatives are both costlier and sometimes equally damaging.

title: Learning a Language Online
passage: Online language courses have grown enormously, and millions of learners now study a foreign language without ever attending a class. Supporters argue that online study is flexible, inexpensive and allows learners to pause and repeat a lesson as often as they need. Sceptics point out that fluency requires conversation with other speakers, and that most free courses stop at the intermediate level. Research on the subject suggests a middle position: online courses are excellent for grammar and vocabulary, yet learners still need regular spoken practice to reach an advanced level. The trend is therefore not the replacement of the classroom, but its extension.
mainIdea: Online courses are excellent for grammar and vocabulary but cannot develop advanced fluency, so they extend rather than replace the classroom.
keyPoints: Millions of learners now study languages online because such courses are flexible, inexpensive and allow unlimited repetition.
Sceptics note that fluency requires real conversation and that free courses usually stop at the intermediate level.
Research suggests online study is strong for grammar and vocabulary but must be combined with regular spoken practice.
reference: Online language courses are flexible, inexpensive and let learners pause and repeat, which is why millions study a language without ever attending a class, yet because fluency still requires regular conversation and free courses rarely exceed the intermediate level, they extend the classroom rather than replace it.

title: Cities That Removed Parking
passage: A number of European cities have converted streets previously used for parking into wider pavements, cycle lanes or public squares. Retailers in these cities often report falling sales at first, and shop owners have mounted visible campaigns against the change. Independent studies have shown, however, that footfall in the affected streets frequently recovers within a year or two and that the new layouts are used by more people overall. The research also finds that the removal of parking frees space that would otherwise be occupied by stationary cars. Most transport planners now regard parking reduction as one of the cheapest ways to improve city streets.
mainIdea: Removing parking frees street space and usually restores footfall within two years, so planners see it as one of the cheapest genuine improvements to city streets.
keyPoints: Several cities have converted parking streets into wider pavements, cycle lanes and public squares.
Retailers reported falling sales first and campaigned against the change, but studies show footfall recovers within a year or two.
Planners note that the change frees space otherwise taken by stationary cars and is among the cheapest improvements available.
reference: Although retailers initially reported falling sales after cities removed parking to build wider pavements, cycle lanes and public squares, independent research shows footfall recovers within two years and planners consider the freed street space one of the cheapest genuine improvements.
